meta.title: Who really said "Give them a whiff of grapeshot"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Napoleon never said it. The phrase "a whiff of grapeshot" was coined by historian Thomas Carlyle in The French Revolution (1837).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Give them a whiff of grapeshot'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Napoleon — Thomas Carlyle coined "a whiff of grapeshot" in his 1837 history of the French Revolution.

answer.label: Not Napoleon Bonaparte — the phrase is Thomas Carlyle's
answer.authorDates: 1795–1881 · Scottish essayist & historian who coined “a whiff of grapeshot”
answer.sourceLine: The phrase was coined by the Scottish historian Thomas Carlyle in The French Revolution: A History (1837) — a whole chapter is titled “The Whiff of Grapeshot.” It is Carlyle’s literary narration for Napoleon’s cannon-fire dispersal of a Paris mob on 13 Vendémiaire (5 Oct 1795), not a command Napoleon ever gave. In the same text Napoleon is quoted only denying he fired blanks first ↗; the imperative “Give them a whiff of grapeshot” is a later paraphrase built on Carlyle’s phrase.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Vol. III, Book VII, ch. VII — “The Whiff of Grapeshot”

source.excerpt: “Singular: in old Broglie’s time, six years ago, this Whiff of Grapeshot was promised; but it could not be given then, could not have profited then.” — and of Napoleon himself Carlyle records only a denial: “It is false,” says Napoleon, “that we fired first with blank charge; it had been a waste of life to do that.”
trail: Carlyle’s primary text ↗ uses “Whiff of Grapeshot” as a chapter title and authorial narration — not as a line spoken by Napoleon.
Wikiquote ↗ files the phrase under Napoleon’s Misattributed section and credits its first use to Carlyle (1837).
Napoleon historian Shannon Selin ↗ lists it among ten famous things Napoleon never said, noting the term was first used by Carlyle.
source.excerptNote: In Carlyle’s narration the phrase is his own; where Napoleon speaks, he says nothing resembling “give them a whiff of grapeshot.”

source.rightsNote: The wording originates in Thomas Carlyle’s The French Revolution: A History, first published in 1837 — well before 1931 — so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Thomas Carlyle
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, satirist and essayist whose vivid, idiosyncratic prose shaped how the Victorian world imagined the past. His three-volume The French Revolution: A History (1837) made his reputation and gave English several enduring phrases — including “the whiff of grapeshot.” By coincidence he was born in December 1795, weeks after the very insurrection the phrase describes.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the most durable things Napoleon never said. The words are a Victorian historian’s, retro-fitted into Napoleon’s mouth as either a battlefield order or a boast.

items.why: The imperative “Give them a whiff of grapeshot” appears in none of Napoleon’s recorded words. In the very source that made the phrase famous, Carlyle quotes Napoleon ↗ only denying he fired blanks first — he never utters the phrase. Wikiquote ↗ lists it as misattributed.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Thomas Carlyle, who coined “the whiff of grapeshot” as his own narration in The French Revolution: A History (1837) ↗.

context.heading: Why the phrase stuck
lead: On 13 Vendémiaire (5 October 1795) a young Napoleon Bonaparte helped the Republic scatter a royalist rising in Paris with point-blank artillery fire — the episode that first made his name. Four decades later, Thomas Carlyle compressed the whole convulsion into a memorable image: the Revolution, he wrote, was ended by “a whiff of grapeshot.”

Carlyle’s phrase was so vivid that it detached from his book and reattached to Napoleon himself, mutating into a supposed order — “give them a whiff of grapeshot” — that no primary source records him giving.
context.pull: The Revolution was “blown into space” by a whiff of grapeshot — Carlyle’s image, not Napoleon’s order.
